questions.stem: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is always such as to

options.text: make the induced e.m.f. as large as possible
flow from south pole to north pole inside the magnet

questions.explanation: Lenz's law is the direction rule that accompanies Faraday's law: the induced current sets up a field that opposes the change of flux. If you push a north pole toward a coil, the near end becomes a north pole and repels the incoming magnet. That opposition is required by conservation of energy.

distractorRationale.a: Aiding the change would give energy for nothing and violate conservation of energy
distractorRationale.c: The size of E is Faraday's second law (rate of change of flux linkage), not Lenz's law
distractorRationale.d: Field lines inside a magnet run S to N, but that is not a statement about induced current

questions.stem: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the

options.text: magnetic flux linked with the circuit
rate of change of magnetic flux linkage
steady current in a nearby wire

questions.explanation: $E = -N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$. A large but unchanging flux induces nothing; a small flux that changes quickly can induce a large e.m.f. That is why flicking a magnet through a coil kicks the galvanometer harder than parking the magnet inside the coil.

distractorRationale.a: Flux itself does not induce an e.m.f.; only a changing flux does. A coil sitting in a steady field has flux but no E
distractorRationale.c: Resistance determines the induced current I = E/R, not the e.m.f. itself
distractorRationale.d: A steady nearby current produces a steady field and therefore no induced e.m.f. Only a changing current would

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT increase the e.m.f. induced in a coil when a magnet is moved through it?

options.text: Increasing the number of turns on the coil
Increasing the resistance of the coil winding

questions.explanation: $E = -N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$. More turns, a faster change and a larger $\Delta\Phi$ (stronger magnet or larger area) all raise $E$. Resistance does not appear in Faraday's law: it affects only the current that the e.m.f. can drive, $I = E/R$. A higher-resistance coil actually gives a smaller induced current.

distractorRationale.a: E is proportional to N, so extra turns increase the induced e.m.f.
distractorRationale.b: Faster motion shortens Δt and so increases the rate of change of flux
distractorRationale.c: A stronger magnet increases ΔΦ for the same motion

questions.stem: A metal rod of length 0.20 m moves at 4.0 m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. Calculate the induced e.m.f. Give your answer in volts.
questions.explanation: When $B$, $l$ and $v$ are mutually perpendicular, $E = Blv = 0.50 \times 0.20 \times 4.0 = 0.40\ \text{V}$. Using $B/l$ or omitting one factor is a common slip; moving the rod parallel to $B$ would give zero because no flux is cut.

questions.stem: A simple a.c. generator uses slip rings rather than a split-ring commutator so that

options.text: the current in the coil itself does not reverse
the connections to the external circuit are not reversed each half-turn, giving alternating output
sparking at the brushes is completely eliminated
the induced e.m.f. becomes steady d.c.

questions.explanation: In the rotating coil the induced e.m.f. already reverses every half-turn. Slip rings keep each brush on the same side of the coil, so that reversal is passed straight to the load — that is a.c. A split ring would swap the connections every half-turn and make the external current one-way (d.c. dynamo).

distractorRationale.a: The current in the coil of any rotating generator reverses; slip rings do not stop that
distractorRationale.c: Brushes on slip rings still spark somewhat; sparking is not the reason for choosing them
distractorRationale.d: Steady (or even pulsing) d.c. is what a split-ring commutator produces, not slip rings

questions.stem: In a simple a.c. generator the induced e.m.f. is a maximum when the plane of the coil is
questions.explanation: Induced e.m.f. depends on how fast the flux is changing, not on how large the flux is. When the coil is parallel to $B$, the flux through it is zero but the wires are cutting field lines at the greatest rate, so $E$ is a maximum. When the coil is perpendicular to $B$, flux is a maximum but $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t = 0$ for that instant, so $E = 0$.

distractorRationale.a: This is the position of maximum flux, which students confuse with maximum e.m.f.; actually E = 0 here
distractorRationale.c: At 45° the e.m.f. has an intermediate value, not its peak
distractorRationale.d: A stationary coil has ΔΦ/Δt = 0 in every orientation, so E = 0

questions.stem: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed toward a closed coil. The induced current in the coil, viewed from the magnet, is such that the near face of the coil

options.text: becomes a south pole, attracting the magnet in
becomes a north pole, repelling the approaching magnet
becomes unmagnetised, because induced fields cancel
produces no pole until the magnet has entered the coil

questions.explanation: The flux through the coil is increasing toward you as the north pole approaches. Lenz's law requires the induced current to oppose that increase, so the near face must itself become a north pole and repel the incoming magnet. You do work against that repulsion; the work appears as electrical energy in the coil.

distractorRationale.a: Attraction would aid the incoming magnet, violating Lenz's law and conservation of energy
distractorRationale.c: A current-carrying coil has a definite field; the induced current does not cancel itself to zero
distractorRationale.d: Induction starts as soon as flux begins to change, which is while the magnet is still approaching

questions.stem: A coil of 200 turns has its flux increased by 0.050 Wb in 0.10 s. Calculate the average induced e.m.f. Give your answer in volts.
questions.explanation: Faraday's law: $E = N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t = 200 \times 0.050 / 0.10 = 10 / 0.10 = 100\ \text{V}$. Forgetting $N$ gives 0.50 V; inverting the time gives 10 V. The minus sign in $E = -N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$ gives direction; the magnitude asked here is 100 V.

distractorRationale.d: A stronger magnetic field results in a greater induced e.m.f. as per Faraday's law.
